_about.what: The air war on the campaign map. An air fleet is a count of fighters and bombers at a base region under a named commander. Left alone it supports the armies and defends its own sky (that support is the Air line on every land Battle Ticket). Given orders it fights a month-long air campaign: winning the sky over a region, bombing industry by day or night, or striking shipping in a sea.
_about.kmPerUnit: Map units to kilometres. Ranges below are in kilometres, measured between region centres.
_about.nations: quality is how well an air force fights, plane for plane. ftrRange is how far its fighters can escort or intercept, bmrRange how far its bombers reach. A fighter is at full effect out to 'fullAt' of its range and falls to 'atLimit' at the limit; beyond that the bombers go alone.
_about.radar: A nation with a radar chain gets warning of raids on its own soil: all its fighters in reach get up in time, and fewer aircraft are caught on the ground. Without radar only 'without' of the defending fighters meet the raid.
_about.production: Aircraft built each month, as [from turn, fighters, bombers]. They go to a reserve and from there to fleets below establishment.
_about.pilots: Fighter pilots trained each month, as [from turn, pilots]. A fighter needs a pilot. 'home' is the share of pilots shot down over friendly ground who fly again; 'away' the share who get home from over enemy ground.
_about.reserve: The most the reserve holds: spare aircraft and spare pilots beyond this go elsewhere.
_about.fleets: est is the establishment over time, as [from turn, fighters, bombers]: the strength a fleet is kept at. When it drops, the surplus goes to the reserve for other fleets. start is the strength on the first day, if below establishment. from is the month the fleet forms, once its base is held. ftrRange gives one fleet's fighters a reach of their own, in place of its nation's: the long-range fighters of 1944. scripted marks an air force history raised for an invasion of its own planning: in free play it does not form. home marks a command that guards its own country: when that country's army goes across an ocean and its air groups follow (world.json 'overseas'), this one stays where it is.
_about.america: The United States (ruling 133(b), Version 84.2). Its commands stand on fields beyond the old chart, so they form only in the grand campaign: the home commands from the first day (about 500 first-line aircraft in September 1939, kept larger from 1941 and smaller again once the air forces overseas are raised), and from June 1942 the air forces raised against Germany. Each is dated by the month history sent it overseas, not the day its headquarters was activated (the Eighth was activated in January 1942 and flew from England that summer): it forms at home at part strength, is filled from the factories and is shipped across with the army, one group a month. The long-range fighter comes with the last of them, at the end of 1943. Its bombers reach 1,100 km. Its air forces in the Pacific wait for the Pacific.
_about.combat: fighters and bombers scale the month's losses. escortShare is how much of the defenders' effort falls on the escort rather than the bombers. bomberDefence is what a bomber's own guns are worth. flak is the share of bombers lost to guns alone. seaCover is how much of a fighter force can cover ships at sea. night: few fighters find the bombers and few bombs find the target.
_about.damage: airfields: bombers needed to cut a base's readiness by 1.0, the most one month can cut, and the share of bombers that destroys an aircraft on the ground. industry: bombers needed to stop a region's output for a month, and the most one month can stop. shipping: how hard a strike falls on ships at sea and on coastal trade.
_about.airfields: The airfields of one region serve 'holds' aircraft. When more are based there, every fleet in the region flies only that share of its aircraft.
_about.sky: The attacker wins the sky over a region when the fighters he has left outweigh, by 'win', the fighters the defender can still put up once his losses are made good. It lasts a month unless won again. land is what it is worth in a land battle there. On a coast, the side that holds the sky counts 'seaOwn' of its air strength over that sea and the other side only 'seaFoe' of its own.
_about.ready: How fit a fleet is to fly, 0 to 1. A fleet at readiness r fights at 0.5 + 0.5 r of its strength.
_about.plan: What computer-run air forces do in Historical mode, month by month. Each order names a fleet, the first base on its list it can use, and a mission. Fleets without orders support their armies and defend.

close._note: Close air support (Brian's ask of 2026-11-18, 18:58Z; the land field thread's seam): a land fighter group given the standing order 'Ground support' flies over its own side's land battles within its fighters' reach, in place of meeting raids and escorting. The grand campaign only, and only while 'on' is true; off, nothing reads this. Each battle a group flies over costs it 'ready' readiness and, per air strike, 'loss' of the aircraft it brings, 'enemySky' times that under the other side's sky; it flies one battle a week, and none below 'least' readiness or in a month it has flown a raid. On the battle card the side's on-call weight W (aircraft x reach x airfields x readiness x technology x fuel) adds most x min(1, W / full) to its side of the air edge, and this term alone reaches past the sky's clamp at 1 (the design director's b536: ground attack paid most where the sky was already won); under the grand campaign's sky row a full term is worth about x1.05 on the attack and x1.03 on the defence; the strikes it makes are W / strike, rounded, between strikes[0] and strikes[1], where it makes at least 'counts' of the side's strength.

ai._note: A staff's ground support (b536 asks for it; behind its own switch 'on', so that the player's choice can be on while every war fought by staffs alone stays as it was): while its main army is on the attack, it puts on ground support the land fighter groups that reach the battles of its main effort, nearest first, up to 'share' of its land fighters (by aircraft); the rest patrol and fly its sweeps and escorts. On the defensive, or while the army is brought up, none.
